title: Baccala Mantecato
subtitle: Venetian whipped salt cod with olive oil
excerpt: Baccala mantecato is the great Venetian salt cod preparation: soaked dried salt cod beaten with olive oil into a pale, fluffy, intensely savoury cream. It is eaten cold, spread on grilled polenta or toasted bread. It appears in every bacaro in Venice as the defining cicchetto.
sourceNotes: Baccala mantecato is one of the defining Venetian dishes. Salt cod (baccala in Venetian -- technically stoccafisso, air-dried stockfish, rather than the salt-cured baccala) arrived in Venice from Norway in the fifteenth century via trade routes. The Venetian method of beating the soaked cod with olive oil to make a creamy paste is unique to the city.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Baccala mantecato keeps in the fridge for 3 days covered with a thin film of olive oil.

content.text: The process is simple but requires 48 hours of soaking to remove the salt from the cod, so plan ahead. The beating technique is what makes baccala mantecato distinctive: the warm, cooked cod is beaten vigorously with olive oil, like a mayonnaise, until it becomes pale, fluffy, and almost airy. The Venetian tradition uses a wooden spoon; a hand mixer works faster and produces an equally good result.

items.prepNote: soaked in cold water for 48 hours, changing the water every 12 hours

content.text: Soak {{salt-cod}} salt cod in a large bowl of cold water for 48 hours, changing the water every 12 hours. The cod will plump up and soften. Taste a small piece after 36 hours -- it should be pleasantly salty but not overwhelmingly so.

Drain the soaked cod and place in a saucepan. Cover with fresh cold water and bring slowly to a bare simmer. Cook for 15 minutes. Do not boil hard or the flesh will tighten. Drain and leave until cool enough to handle. Remove the skin and all bones. Flake the flesh into a large bowl.

While the cod is still warm, beat it vigorously with a hand mixer or wooden spoon. Drizzle in {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} olive oil in a thin stream while beating, exactly as if making mayonnaise. Continue until the mixture is pale, fluffy, and holds soft peaks. Add {{garlic}} garlic paste if using and {{black-pepper}} pepper. A splash of {{lemon}} lemon juice can be added to brighten the flavour.
Spread onto grilled polenta or toasted bread. Scatter {{parsley-flat}} parsley over and serve at room temperature.

items.symptom: The mixture is grainy rather than fluffy
items.cause: The cod was too cold when beaten, or the oil was added too quickly.
items.fix: Beat the cod while still warm and add the oil very slowly, a drop at a time at first, exactly as when making mayonnaise. Cold cod does not emulsify well. If it splits, add a tablespoon of warm water and beat again.

content.text: Baccala mantecato is one of the oldest Venetian dishes. The cod used in Venice is technically Norwegian stockfish -- air-dried rather than salt-cured -- and arrived via northern trade routes in the fifteenth century. The German trading house on the Grand Canal was the point of entry for much of this fish. The technique of beating the cooked cod with olive oil until fluffy is unique to Venice and is found nowhere else in Italy.
